games.canonical_title: The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time
Grand Theft Auto: San Andreas - The Definitive Edition

aliases.alias: the legend of zelda ocarina of time

sections.name: Glyphid Dreadnought
sections.card: Kite between waves; focus weak-point armor plates as they open. Save overclock/nuke for armor break windows.

sections.name: Hollow Bough
sections.card: Sticky webs and reduced visibility — mobility build or clear web shooters first. XP magnet perks help swarm waves.

sections.name: Tank
sections.card: The big one, the one throwing chunks of concrete at you. While he is up the director stops sending commons and specials outside finales, so it is four guns against one target — but slip past him and the horde comes straight back. Fight him in the open: anything he can punch becomes a projectile with more reach than his fists, and a punch taken near a drop kills rather than knocks down. If the route makes him crouch through a vent he is barely mobile, and he never looks for another way round.

sections.name: The Parish
sections.card: Hold choke points with shotguns; watch rooftop crescendo timing. Medkits before the finale wave.

sections.name: Mind Flayer
sections.card: Break concentration and interrupt psychic links. Position to avoid AoE after each phase shift.

sections.name: Goblin Camp
sections.card: Use elevation and stealth for surprise rounds. Short rest before multi-wave camp defense.

sections.name: Deathclaw
sections.card: Very high health for its level and resistant to nearly everything, energy weapons worst of all — lasers can reflect straight off the hide. It opens with a roar and a ground stomp, headbutts to stagger, and throws cars at you once you are out of reach. Below a certain health it can kill you outright with a grab or a decapitation, and at low level that threshold is higher than it sounds, so distance and cover matter more than raw damage.

sections.name: Corvega Factory
sections.card: Clear raiders floor-by-floor; grenades for clustered groups. Save ammo for Assaultron encounter.

sections.name: Downtown
sections.card: PCSX2: stable 60 FPS needs aggressive EE/IOP tuning. EmuDeck preset recommended for Deck.

sections.name: Final Confrontation
sections.card: Stock riot gear pickups; keep crowd control weapons for riot phases.

sections.name: Megara
sections.card: Learn dash patterns; punish recovery windows. Mirror and trap boons help burst phases.

sections.name: Temple of Styx
sections.card: Buy charms before entry; poison resistance or healing crucial. Route choice affects shop access.

sections.name: Adam Smasher
sections.card: Sandevistan or high DPS builds; destroy legs first. Cover during rocket barrages.

sections.name: All Foods Plant
sections.card: Stealth route saves ammo; quickhack turrets when detected. Deck: lower crowd density settings help FPS.

sections.name: Big Smoke
sections.card: Keep distance during chase; aim for vehicle weak points. Motorcycle section: avoid collisions.

sections.name: Los Santos
sections.card: DE edition: verify Proton forced; shader cache regen after updates. Driving missions: cap FPS for stability.

sections.name: Starter Lot
sections.card: Build small starter home first; career goals unlock skills. Deck: lower sim speed in crowded lots.

sections.name: Get a Job
sections.card: Complete daily tasks for steady income before expanding house. Save before major lot changes.

sections.name: Bear
sections.card: Dead Eye on entry; headshots during slow. Use cover trees; horse keeps distance.

sections.name: Valentine
sections.card: Honor missions affect town mood. Stable upkeep and camp supplies before long hunts.

sections.name: Gels
sections.card: Three paints, all useless on glass. Blue bounces you higher the further you fell. Orange removes friction so you keep whatever speed you arrive with. White lets you portal a surface that refused portals before, but it will not stick to cubes or turrets, and the cleansing spray strips it.

sections.name: Repulsion Gel
sections.card: The blue one. Bounce height scales with how far you dropped, so gain height by falling onto it from somewhere higher, not by jumping. Two coated surfaces facing each other let you climb by bouncing between them.

sections.name: Aerial Faith Plate
sections.card: Launches to a fixed destination, but it keeps the speed you arrive with — so run or fall into one to travel further than it looks. It throws objects as well as you, and its arc can be fed through a portal.

sections.name: Hard Light Bridge
sections.card: Solid light that runs until something blocks it. Put a portal in its path to move the whole bridge somewhere else — it leaves the portal square-on, so centre the portal on the beam. It is also cover: a turret cannot see through it, let alone shoot. Gel sits on a bridge and disappears when the bridge does.

sections.name: Excursion Funnel
sections.card: Weightless travel along the beam. If it is carrying you the wrong way, look for the button that reverses it before assuming the route is shut. It passes through portals, so it can cross the whole chamber, and it ferries gel and cubes as well as you.

sections.name: Thermal Discouragement Beam
sections.card: The laser exists to feed receptacles and relays; the exit usually will not open until it reaches one. A redirection cube aims it freely, portals only along fixed directions, and it goes straight through glass. Held on a turret, it cooks it.

sections.name: Wheatley
sections.card: He strips the portal surfaces, shields himself and throws bombs. Let a bomb break the conversion gel pipe, paint a wall with what spills, and portal his own bombs back into him. Every stun buys time to attach one corrupted core; three of them force the transfer.

sections.name: Co-op portals and pinging
sections.card: Two players, two guns, four portals — and a portal one of you places links with the other's, which is the whole puzzle most of the time. Ping to point at a spot or to count down a timed jump; it carries without voice chat. Dying costs nothing but seconds.

sections.name: Co-op courses
sections.card: Five courses unlock in order — Team Building, then Mass and Velocity, Hard-Light Surfaces, Excursion Funnels and Mobility Gels — each teaching one mechanic before combining them. Art Therapy is the DLC course after those.

sections.name: Gravity Gun
sections.card: Secondary pulls and holds, primary punts. Explosive barrels hit hardest, sawblades cut zombies apart, and a held radiator works as a shield you can walk behind. It will not lift most enemies, but manhacks and scanners are fair game, and thrown grenades can go back where they came from.

sections.name: Ravenholm
sections.card: Ammo is scarce on purpose, so fight with the town instead of your guns. Levers drop car traps and reset them; waist-high blade traps shred zombies while you duck under; propane spray ignites from a single shot. Poison zombies switch traps off, so deal with those first. Loose blades are gravity gun ammunition.

sections.name: Strider
sections.card: RPG only, and roughly seven rockets on Normal. The rocket stays laser-guided the whole flight, so steer it wide and bring it in off-axis rather than straight up the barrel. Its warp cannon does splash damage, so keep moving between shots. A crate of rockets nearby means the fight is a long one.

sections.name: Rocket-Propelled Grenade Launcher
sections.card: Three rockets carried, and every one is steerable — hold the laser where you want it and the rocket follows, even turning right around after a miss. A gunship shoots rockets out of the air, so loop yours around behind it instead of flying it in straight.

sections.name: Antlions
sections.card: Antlions are blind and hunt vibration, so on the coast the rocks are safe and the sand is not — step off and they come up.

sections.name: Pheropod (bugbait)
sections.card: Once you have the pheropod from the Antlion Guard the antlions reverse: throw it and they read you as a guard and swarm whatever you marked.

sections.name: Sandtraps
sections.card: The coastal chapter that teaches the sand. Rock to rock on the way out; after the Antlion Guard you keep the pheropod and use antlions to break the Combine bunkers guarding the road to Nova Prospekt.

sections.name: Hunter-Chopper (helicopter)
sections.card: Fought from the airboat once its gun is mounted. Hold fire on it and pieces break away until it goes down. It drops contact mines and charges a pulse turret between passes; nearly dead, it makes one bombing run, so steer between the lines of falling bombs rather than trying to outrun them.

sections.name: Combine soldiers
sections.card: They move in squads of four to six and will flank you while the rest lay down covering fire, so holding one angle gets you surrounded. A grenade breaks them out of cover and into the open — and you can throw theirs back. Kill the shotgun one first and keep your distance from the rest; up close they club you.

sections.name: The Witch
sections.card: She ignores gunfire that is not aimed at her and ignores other infected; what wakes her is a flashlight or a survivor standing too close. The growl is a warning — back off and she settles. Keep coming and she stands, flails, then charges and incapacitates whoever she picked in one hit. Fire kills her in about fifteen seconds and slows her down, but only once she is already startled: light a wandering witch while she is still calm and she keeps full speed. Either way she switches to whoever burned her, not whoever woke her.

sections.name: Charger
sections.card: Shoving does nothing to him — only explosives stumble him. Treat the charge like a bull: once he commits he cannot steer, so step aside and let him hit a wall. The damage is not the problem, the destination is; near water, a ledge, or a bunched-up team he flings everybody. AI chargers take about two thirds less damage while charging, so wait until he stops rather than emptying a magazine into the run.

sections.name: Hunter
sections.card: He goes for whoever is on their own, and a long pounce does damage before the clawing starts. There is about a second to shove him out of the air, which is more warning than the jockey gives, and he has very little health once you land shots. A pounce does not end on its own — a teammate has to shove him off — so the real counter is not being the survivor at the back.

sections.name: Smoker
sections.card: The cough and the drifting green trails say he has spawned; the tongue says where. Follow it back and shoot: while he is dragging someone he stands still and takes extra damage in campaign, so one headshot ends it. If the tongue pulls the victim against an obstacle it starts choking them, so cut it fast rather than trading shots at range.

sections.name: Jockey
sections.card: The laugh is the warning. Do not swing at him mid-leap — he is much harder to hit than a hunter — step backwards as he jumps and he sails past, then shove and kill him. His damage is slow; the danger is where he steers you, which is into a witch, into acid, into a tank you were not ready for, or off a ledge.

sections.name: Boomer
sections.card: The vomit is not damage, it is a horde sent to you, and killing him at close range coats you anyway because he bursts. Shove first, then shoot. On Easy and Normal there is a second or so of warning; on Advanced and Expert he pukes on sight and backing away does not beat the arc. Being biled makes you glow to both teams, and the burst stumbles anything nearby — chargers and tanks included.

sections.name: Spitter
sections.card: The green puddle burns worse the longer it has been down, and one spit can take most of a survivor's health. Moving out of it is always right, even onto worse ground — including when you are picking someone up, because reviving means standing in it. This is why a jockey ride or a charger pin over acid is lethal rather than annoying.

sections.name: The Director
sections.card: Nothing about the spawns is fixed. Hordes of ten to thirty commons come at you every one to four minutes, from behind or off to the side, while tanks and witches only appear at threat spots the map author placed. After a heavy fight it goes quiet for roughly thirty to forty-five seconds — that pause is the healing window, and moving on ends it early. If the idle commons have thinned out, it is making room for something.

sections.name: Going down and black and white
sections.card: Going down leaves you with 300 temporary health draining three at a time until somebody picks you up. Go down a second time without healing and the screen turns grey with a heartbeat: the third one kills, and only a first aid kit clears it — pills and adrenaline do not. Death is still recoverable, by defibrillator, by reaching the safe room, or from a rescue closet, but Realism switches the closets off.

sections.name: Bile bomb
sections.card: Crowd control, not a weapon. Wherever the jar lands pulls the horde for about twenty seconds, and any infected caught in it gets attacked by its own side. Throw it well away from the team before starting a crescendo, or to buy a route past a tank — not at whatever is closest.

sections.name: Expert and Realism
sections.card: Two different kinds of hard. On Expert a single common does 20 a hit, standing still gets you killed, and a tank punch incapacitates outright. Realism is a separate switch that works on any difficulty: no outlines around your teammates, no item glow, no rescue closets, and commons shrug off body shots, so it is headshots, melee, or the magnum. Learn a map with Realism off first — the director puts supplies off the obvious path.

sections.name: Playing as the Tank
sections.card: Save him for ground that suits him: mounted guns shred you, so go around rather than through, and wait for the rest of the infected team to be up before you commit. Rocks are for the places they must walk through. Chase the panicking one or the biled one rather than the nearest one, and if a teammate has someone pinned, put your body between that survivor and their friends — the bullets hitting you are bullets not saving them. Someone running at you with a revved chainsaw gets punched before they arrive.

sections.name: Playing as the Hunter
sections.card: Pounce damage scales with distance — up to 25 on a long one — so height and a run-up matter more than surprise alone. Take the straggler, never the group, and if you have to be near the group, move like a common: the melee claw reads as horde damage until someone checks. In Left 4 Dead 2 the pounce recharges fast, so holding crouch and re-pouncing keeps pressure on.

sections.name: Playing as the Jockey
sections.card: The ride is the weapon. Steer towards a witch, a spitter pool, a fire, a ledge or an unfinished tank fight — anywhere the survivor's own team makes things worse. Rides last longer where the map turns: corners, alleys, stairwells. Off a ledge is only worth it when nobody is close enough to pick them back up, otherwise a charger does that job better.

sections.name: Playing as the Smoker
sections.card: Patience, then elevation. Wait until the team is busy, then take someone from above — a drop adds fall damage on top of the 3 a second the tongue does, and a hanging victim is far harder to rescue than one dragged along the floor. Pull towards a witch, a fire, or a drop rather than towards yourself; you have no cover. Keep moving, because standing still leaves a green cloud that marks you.

sections.name: Playing as the Charger
sections.card: Angle beats timing. A hallway lets you bowl the whole team at once; open ground lets you carry one of them far enough that the rescue costs the others real time. A drop or a hazard on the line turns the charge into a kill outright. Check nothing solid is between you and the target — hitting it stops you dead — and do not spawn early, because the grunting gives away the ambush.

sections.name: Playing as the Boomer
sections.card: Support, not damage. Set up out of sight, let them walk into range rather than charging in, and spawn just before you puke so the noise does not give you away. Bile on a grouped, distracted team while your teammates are ready is worth more than bile on whoever is nearest. Exploding on purpose in the middle of the mess is a legitimate second use.

sections.name: Playing as the Spitter
sections.card: Put the acid where they have to walk — a doorway, an alley, the stairs off a ledge — not in open ground they can step around. Spit from a balcony or a dark corner, since a headshot usually kills you outright and the glow gives you away in the light. Best paired with the horde: near a car alarm or a crowd, the pool is what stops them dealing with either.

sections.name: Sandevistan
sections.card: An operating system rather than one more implant, and it is built around blades — it slows time on demand, and some variants add crit chance and crit damage on top. Mods extend the duration or shorten the cooldown. Since patch 2.0 you can switch it off early by pressing the button again instead of burning the tail of it.

sections.name: Berserk
sections.card: The other operating system, and the melee one that does not care about time. While it runs it cuts damage taken and will not let your health fall below a quarter, and afterwards every enemy you put down returns a quarter of your maximum health. What it does for your melee weapons depends on the model installed.

sections.name: Kerenzikov
sections.card: Lets you fire while sliding, dodging or dashing, and aiming during any of those slows time for a couple of seconds. It has its own cooldown, so treat it as a repositioning tool rather than something to lean on.

sections.name: Street Cred
sections.card: A separate track from your character level, paid out by fixers for gigs, and how you finish a job changes the payout rather than just finishing it. It buys a permanent vendor discount up to 15% and unlocks better cars on the Autofixer; the good gear starts appearing around Street Cred 40, and it caps at 50.

sections.name: Lifepath
sections.card: Nomad, Streetkid or Corpo. What it changes is the opening chapter, one unique side job, and dialogue options that keep turning up later on — so pick the opening you want to play rather than the one that sounds strongest.

sections.name: Cyberpsychos
sections.card: Cyberpsychosis is what happens when someone takes on more chrome than they can carry: they stop identifying with people and start seeing them as weak and inferior. A cyberpsycho has the strength and speed all that hardware buys and no regard for their own life or anyone else's, which makes them dangerous out of proportion to where you meet them. There is no talking one down — Night City's answer is MaxTac, a police unit that exists to put them down with overwhelming force.

sections.name: Ripperdocs
sections.card: Ripperdocs are the technicians who install cyberware, somewhere between a surgeon, a techie and a tattoo artist. Most operate legally; some will fit illegal military-grade hardware for the right price. The cheap ones in Little China or out past Rancho Coronado will happily chip you a second-hand piece of junk with a virus thrown in free. Corporate rippers are free and spotless, which is fine if you trust the people you work for with access to your brain.

sections.name: Quickhacks
sections.card: Quickhacks are programs you install in a cyberdeck and fire at enemies or devices. Each costs RAM, takes an upload time before it lands, and runs for a set duration, so a netrunner build is really a question of how much RAM you have and how quickly it comes back. Combat hacks do damage, control hacks disable, covert hacks keep you undetected and cost the least, and ultimates are the strongest and the most expensive. Buy them from netrunner vendors, loot them from enemy netrunners, or win them out of Breach Protocol.

sections.name: Iconic weapons
sections.card: The unique named weapons, usually tied to a character or a quest rather than found in a shop. Each has an effect no other weapon has, and each can be upgraded to keep pace with your level instead of being outgrown. That is why holding on to one you like generally beats chasing bigger numbers on a random drop.

sections.name: Choosing a build
sections.card: Attributes decide more than perks do, so the early choice worth thinking about is which two to raise. Body and Reflexes make a straightforward fighter and forgive mistakes. Intelligence is the netrunner route: quickhacks do the work before a fight starts, but you are fragile once one begins badly. Technical Ability quietly helps every build, because it opens crafting and the cyberware you actually want. Cool rewards patience and stealth and punishes being caught. Spreading points evenly is the one choice that reliably goes badly — the perks worth having sit behind attribute thresholds, and an even spread reaches none of them.

sections.name: Muscle
sections.card: Built at a gym or by running, cycling and swimming — fourteen seconds on the treadmill or bike is one percent, and a weights rep is one percent. It raises melee damage, respect and sex appeal, but do not max it: at 100% it works against sex appeal and some girlfriends will not talk to you. All fifty oysters, expensive clothes and a good car offset that.

sections.name: Stamina
sections.card: Endurance for sprinting, swimming and cycling; low stamina means you stop running almost immediately. It goes up with the activity itself — five percent per two and a half minutes of swimming, or per five minutes of running or biking — and four percent per fourteen seconds on gym cardio. Finishing the Burglary side missions, ten thousand dollars of stolen goods, grants unlimited stamina regardless of the stat.

sections.name: Fat
sections.card: Goes up with food, including meals on dates, and down with exercise or with not eating. Overweight slows you down and costs health, jumping and speed. Zero fat is worse: once there is nothing left to burn you start losing muscle, and after that health, so eat when the hunger warning appears.

sections.name: Respect
sections.card: Sets how many gang members you can recruit, from one up to seven. It comes from missions, killing rival gang members and police, taking territory and spraying over tags, and appearance nudges it — hair, tattoos, clothes, muscle, and wearing green in Grove Street territory most of all. It falls if you wear the wrong colours at home, kill your own, or lose turf.

sections.name: Weapon skill
sections.card: Each weapon type levels separately by hitting people and vehicles: Poor, then Gangster, then Hitman. Higher skill means better accuracy, more range, faster strafing and fire rate, and the ability to move while shooting. At Hitman the pistol, sawn-off, Tec-9 and Micro SMG can be dual wielded. Thrown weapons, melee, rifles and heavy weapons have no skill meter at all.

sections.name: Gang territory
sections.card: Opens up after Sweet's mission Doberman, and goes away for a stretch in the middle of the story before coming back. Holding turf pays: money accumulates and is collected outside the Johnson house on Grove Street, respect goes up, and rival gang members stop spawning in the streets you own.

sections.name: Girlfriends
sections.card: Six of them, and only Millie is actually required for full completion — the rest are optional. Denise and Millie arrive through story missions; Michelle, Katie and Helena become available once Flint County, Whetstone and San Fierro are open, and Barbara once Tierra Robada, Bone County and Las Venturas are. Sex appeal decides whether they will talk to you at all, and all fifty oysters covers most of that.

sections.name: Lung capacity and oysters
sections.card: How long you last underwater. It grows with time spent under, and collecting oysters is the fast way — there are fifty, along shorelines, under bridges and in pools. Let the oxygen meter empty and you lose health quickly, and surfacing gives the air back but not the health. One mission, Amphibious Assault, will not start below five percent lung capacity.

sections.name: Horseshoes
sections.card: Fifty of them around Las Venturas, and all fifty are required for 100% completion. Each one is a hundred dollars and twenty points of luck, a stat that starts at zero and only ever goes up; the full set maxes it at 1,000.

sections.name: Settlement happiness
sections.card: Happiness is just whether needs are met: food, water, beds and defense each have to be at least the number of settlers. Power is not part of it, though better machines need it. Higher happiness makes settlers more productive, and a settlement left very unhappy can be lost outright after a failed Minutemen radiant quest.

sections.name: Settlement defense and attacks
sections.card: One unit of defense per settler is the number to hit, and only workshop-built defenses count — mines do not, though they still kill attackers if you are there. Attack chance rises with stored food and water and falls with population and defense, but never below 2%; a settlement with nobody living in it is never attacked. Turn up in person and it is a normal fight with your turrets and companions helping; skip it and the game rolls defense rating plus population against the raid, which is why spreading defense thin costs you inventory and temporary happiness rather than nothing.

sections.name: SPECIAL points
sections.card: You start with one in everything and 21 to spend, so 28 in total — much less than earlier Fallouts. It is not a permanent ceiling: bobbleheads and magazines raise attributes, and each level-up lets you put the point into a SPECIAL stat instead of a perk. Your SPECIAL values are what decide which perks you can take at all.

sections.name: Perks
sections.card: The perk chart replaced skills. Every level gives one point, and it buys either a rank of a perk or a rank of the SPECIAL attribute that unlocks deeper perks in that column. Magazines scattered around the world grant extra perks that cost no points at all, and they are listed separately on the Pip-Boy.

sections.name: Power armor and fusion cores
sections.card: The frame runs on a fusion core that drains with time and faster with anything that spends AP — sprinting, V.A.T.S. When it empties you can still walk, but you are over-encumbered and lose V.A.T.S. and steady aim. No training perk is needed. Wearing it overrides your normal armour bonuses entirely and can push Strength past the usual limit of 10.

sections.name: Upgrading power armor
sections.card: Repairs and mods happen at a power armor station, and one can be built at a settlement. Upgrading a piece costs the same materials whichever tier you come from, so it is usually worth waiting until Armorer and Science are ranked up rather than paying twice — especially for the later models, whose materials are rare.

sections.name: Mirelurk queen
sections.card: Much bigger and much harder than the rest, doing heavy physical and radiation damage, and her arrival is announced by a roar. On top of the claws she spits acid that keeps damaging you after it lands, and she periodically fires a barrage of eggs that hatch into a wave of small ones — the game treats that as a grenade, so the grenade warning icon is the cue to move.

sections.name: Crafting and junk
sections.card: Almost nothing needs a schematic; the recipes are known by default. What you need is components, which come from scrapping junk at a crafting table, from scrapping world objects such as trees and cars inside a settlement you own, or from merchants. Components are drawn either from your own inventory or from the workshop of the settlement you are standing in.

sections.name: Choosing a build
sections.card: Your S.P.E.C.I.A.L. points at the start matter more than anything picked later, because the perks sit underneath them. Intelligence is the quiet strong pick: it raises how fast you level, so every other perk arrives sooner. Strength with Endurance makes a melee or heavy-weapons survivor that forgives mistakes. Agility with Perception is the sniper and V.A.T.S. route, which kills things before they arrive and folds if they get through. Charisma is the settlement and speech build and is the weakest of the five early, though it pays off later. Every stat can still be raised with bobbleheads and level-ups, so pick for the first ten hours being enjoyable rather than optimising a character you have not met yet.

sections.name: Feral ghouls
sections.card: Irradiated former humans, fast, and they almost never travel alone. The head is the reliable weakness. Take a leg off one and it stops attacking altogether, while taking both arms off does not. They lie among rubble playing dead and climb out of ductwork and windows, so a room that looks clear often is not — though while one is still climbing in it cannot fight back. They deal radiation damage as well as physical, and in heavily irradiated places like the Glowing Sea they regenerate as you shoot them.

sections.name: Stimpaks and chems
sections.card: A stimpak heals a share of your health rather than a flat amount, and repairs crippled limbs. The Medic perk is what makes them worth carrying: across its ranks it takes the heal from 30% up to 100% and speeds the injection up. Two things change in Survival mode and both matter — a stimpak takes fifty seconds to work instead of five, and it starts having weight. Healing mid-fight stops being an option there; you have to break contact first.

sections.name: Legendary enemies
sections.card: A legendary enemy has a star beside its name and is otherwise an ordinary creature with a much deeper health bar. What catches people out is the mutation: at around half health it heals itself completely and gains a new ability, so the fight is roughly twice as long as it first looks and spending everything on the first half is the mistake. Each one drops a weapon or armour piece carrying a random legendary effect, which is the main way good gear enters a playthrough.

sections.name: Queen Gohma
sections.card: The spider in the Deku Tree. She is only vulnerable when the big eye turns red — a slingshot seed or a Deku nut at that moment drops her, and then you get a few free sword slashes before she recovers. When she climbs the ceiling, watch where she lands rather than chasing her.

sections.name: Volvagia
sections.card: The fire dragon that pops out of the holes in the floor. The Megaton Hammer is the whole fight: hit the head the moment it comes up, then slash while it is stunned. When it flies around the room, the hookshot pulls it back down. Goron Tunic and a shield for the fire, and keep off the lava at the edges.

sections.name: Twinrova
sections.card: The two witches, one ice and one fire. First phase, the Mirror Shield reflects each sister's magic into the other — aim at the one who did not cast. Once they merge, the shield absorbs their blasts instead: take three of the same element and it fires back at them. Mixing the elements resets the charge, so wait rather than catching whatever comes.

sections.name: Epona
sections.card: Learn Epona's Song from Malon at Lon Lon Ranch as a child. As an adult, Ingo has taken over — pay to ride, then race him, and he will bet the horse on a rematch. Win that and he locks the gate, so ride at the fence and jump it.

sections.name: Shadow Temple invisible floors
sections.card: Almost everything in the Shadow Temple that looks missing is there. Equip the Lens of Truth and the invisible floors, walls and chests all appear; it drains magic while held, so use it in bursts rather than leaving it on. Green potions and the fairies in the temple keep it running.

sections.name: Adult dungeon order
sections.card: Forest, then Fire, then Water, then Shadow, then Spirit. Each one hands you the item the next expects — the hookshot from Forest, the Megaton Hammer from Fire, the longshot from Water — so going out of order mostly means walking back later. The Spirit Temple is the only one that splits across child and adult.

sections.name: Gold Skulltulas
sections.card: A hundred tokens across the game, and the cursed family in Kakariko pays out every ten: wallet upgrades early, then better rewards, with the last one at a hundred. Ten and twenty are quick and worth doing on the way past. The full hundred is a completionist job, not something to detour for mid-playthrough.

sections.name: Biggoron's Sword
sections.card: A long trade chain that starts with the Pocket Egg from the Cucco Lady in Kakariko and ends at the top of Death Mountain. Two links in it are on a timer — the Odd Mushroom and the Eyedrops — so ride Epona and use the warp songs for those two rather than walking. Everything before and after can be done at your own pace.

sections.name: Mirror of Night
sections.card: The permanent upgrades, bought with Darkness in your room. Each row has two alternatives and you can switch between them for a small cost at any time, so nothing is locked in. Death Defiance is the one that changes early runs most: each rank is another free revive mid-run.

sections.name: Weapon aspects
sections.card: Each weapon has alternate aspects, bought with Titan Blood, that change how it plays rather than just its numbers — a different attack, a different special, sometimes a different role entirely. The last aspect for each weapon unlocks later in the story. Judging a weapon by its starting form alone is why people write one off early.

sections.name: Stygian Blade
sections.card: The safest thing to learn on — short reach, forgiving timing, and a three-hit combo that recovers quickly enough to get out of. Its dash-strike closes distance, so you can play it aggressively without committing to standing still. If you do not know which to take, take this one.

sections.name: Shield of Chaos
sections.card: The most survivable weapon, because holding block turns a mistake into nothing rather than reducing it. Blocking also sets up a rush that closes distance and hits hard, so defence and offence are the same button. A good pick for a boss you keep dying to.

sections.name: Heart-Seeking Bow
sections.card: Rewards staying at range and punishes standing still. Shots charge before they fire, so the rhythm is back away, charge, release — firing early is what makes the bow feel weak. Its special fires a spread that works close up, which is the answer when something reaches you.

sections.name: Eternal Spear
sections.card: The longest reach of the six, which is the whole point of it — you can hit things before they are in range to hit you. Its spin attack sweeps everything around you and is the answer to being surrounded. The special throws the spear and pulls it back, hitting on the way out and the way in.

sections.name: Twin Fists of Malphon
sections.card: The fastest weapon and the shortest reach, so it asks you to stand inside everything. Because it lands so many hits, it stacks boons that trigger on hit far faster than anything else — which is what makes it strong once you know what you are doing, and punishing before then.

sections.name: Adamant Rail
sections.card: A gun, so it has a magazine and a reload — the one weapon where running dry at the wrong moment is what kills you. It rewards staying at range and punishes standing still. Its special lobs a bomb, so unlike the bow it has an answer to a crowd.

sections.name: Weapon choice
sections.card: Take the Stygian Blade first: it is the most forgiving of the six and asks the least of you. The Shield of Chaos is the next easiest, because holding block turns a mistake into nothing. Of the rest, the Eternal Spear is the safest, since its reach keeps you out of trouble. Leave the Twin Fists of Malphon until later — they are the fastest, but they need you standing inside everything. The Heart-Seeking Bow and the Adamant Rail both want range and punish standing still, and the Rail can leave you reloading at the worst possible moment.

sections.name: Darkness, keys and gems
sections.card: They are different currencies for different things: Darkness feeds the Mirror, Chthonic Keys unlock new weapons and new Mirror rows, and gems pay for the house contractor. Early on, keys and Darkness are both bottlenecks — take whichever you have fewer of, and stop taking gems once the contractor jobs you want are bought.

sections.name: Boons and duo boons
sections.card: Boons come from gods and last one run. A duo needs two specific gods' boons already in the right slots, so you cannot aim at one directly — you pick a god early, keep taking them, and the duo becomes possible. Taking one boon from every god who offers is how runs end up with nothing that stacks.

sections.name: Theseus and Asterius
sections.card: Two at once, which is the actual difficulty. Asterius, the bull, telegraphs a long charge — sidestep it and he is briefly stuck. Theseus throws his spear and periodically calls down a god's power, which is marked on the ground before it lands. Most runs go better killing Asterius first, because Theseus alone is predictable.

sections.name: Heat and the Pact of Punishment
sections.card: Beating the game once is the middle of the story, not the end — the runs continue and the ending needs several more. The Pact of Punishment unlocks then too: Heat is optional difficulty you add yourself, in exchange for rewards that only come from raising it.

sections.name: Long rest
sections.card: Rest more than feels right. A long rest costs camp supplies and restores spells, health and most abilities, and it is also what advances companion scenes and personal quests — hoarding rests means missing story, not saving resources. Supplies are plentiful; food you pick up counts.

sections.name: Inspiration
sections.card: Each character has background goals, and doing something that matches one grants Inspiration. You can hold a few at a time, and spending one rerolls a failed ability check — including in dialogue, after you have seen the failure. Picking backgrounds that suit how you actually play is what keeps the supply up.

sections.name: Dialogue checks
sections.card: A check is your ability modifier plus proficiency plus a d20, so the fix is usually who is talking rather than luck: let the high-Charisma character lead conversations. The Guidance cantrip adds a d4 to a check and can be cast beforehand, and Inspiration rerolls a failure outright.

sections.name: Companion approval
sections.card: Companions react to what you do and say in front of them, not to gifts. Approval gates their personal quests and any romance, and low approval can end with them leaving. Someone who disapproves of a plan can be left at camp for it.

sections.name: Sneak Attack
sections.card: Sneak Attack needs advantage, or an ally already next to the target — without one of those it is a normal, weak attack. Hide as a bonus action, attack from stealth, and let a melee companion engage first. Height and darkness help too: shooting from above and out of sight is the rogue's normal opening, not a trick.

sections.name: Party composition
sections.card: Four slots. You want someone to talk, someone to heal, someone who can find and disarm traps and pick locks, and enough damage — one character often covers two of those. Bard and Paladin both talk well; Cleric and Druid both heal; Rogue and Ranger both handle traps. The party you cannot cover is the one with no healing at all.

sections.name: Honor
sections.card: It moves on small things done often: greeting people, helping strangers on the road, paying bounties instead of running, donating to camp. It falls for robbery, killing civilians and animals you do not use. High honor means shop discounts and different reactions; low honor pays differently. It is a slider, not a switch — one bad day does not undo a good chapter.

sections.name: Horse bonding
sections.card: Bond level is what makes a horse feel different. Riding, feeding, brushing, patting and calming it during danger all raise it, and each level adds stamina, better handling, and eventually manoeuvres like the rear and the drift. A high-bond horse also stops throwing you when something scares it. Bond is per horse, so switching mounts starts again.

sections.name: Cores and rings
sections.card: Each of health, stamina and Dead Eye has an inner core and a ring around it. The ring is the meter you spend; the core is the reserve that refills it, and it drains from hunger, cold and injury. Eat and sleep to keep cores up, and use tonics for the rings mid-fight. A dead core means everything drains faster, which is what makes long rides go wrong.

sections.name: Dead Eye
sections.card: Slows time and refills from tonics, food and clean kills. Early on it auto-marks; later story upgrades let you paint targets yourself and eventually see weak points. Use it for the shot you cannot line up rather than for every fight, because the meter is a resource and not a mode.

sections.name: Perfect pelts
sections.card: Two things have to be true: a three-star animal, and a clean kill with the right weapon for its size. Small animals want the varmint rifle; medium ones want a bow with improved arrows; big ones want a rifle to the head or heart. Study an animal first to see its rating, and skin it or take the carcass to a trapper or butcher before it spoils.

sections.name: Bounties
sections.card: A bounty stays on the region it was earned in and grows with witnesses. Leave it and lawmen and bounty hunters keep coming, and a big enough one effectively closes that region's towns to you. Pay it at any post office; wearing a mask during a crime keeps the bounty smaller.

sections.name: Camp donations
sections.card: The ledger is not a tax — it is where camp upgrades come from, and they are real: better provisions, more ammo and food to take for free, faster fast travel from camp once bought. Contributing also keeps morale up. Money given to the ledger goes further than money in your pocket for most of the early game.

sections.name: Legendary animals
sections.card: There is one legendary animal per species, each in a fixed place on the map, and each drops a pelt no ordinary animal gives. The Trapper is the only person who turns those pelts into clothing; the fence takes the trinkets. They absorb far more punishment than a normal animal of the same size, so bring a rifle matched to the target rather than whatever is already in your hands.

sections.name: Tonics and provisions
sections.card: Health, stamina and Dead Eye each sit on top of a core, and eating and tonics act on both parts. Food keeps the cores from draining; tonics refill the bar, and the gold-labelled ones also fortify the core so it drains more slowly for a while. Carry a few of each before a long ride or a fight — most early deaths are somebody with a full satchel who never opened it.

sections.name: Horse breeds
sections.card: Breeds differ in speed, in stamina, and in how easily they spook at gunfire or predators. Draft horses carry more and panic less but are slow; racing breeds are quick and fragile. Arabians and the war breeds are the ones worth saving for, though an Arabian bolts easily until its bond comes up. Early on the bond matters more than the stat line: a bonded horse handles better and comes when you whistle from further away.

sections.name: Satchel upgrades
sections.card: Pearson crafts satchel upgrades at camp once you bring him the pelts and the camp can afford it, and each tier raises how much of everything you can carry. The last one, the Legend of the East satchel, wants perfect pelts from a long list of animals, which is the real reason people care about clean kills. Upgrading early is worth more than it sounds, because running out of room is what stops most people restocking before they ride out.

sections.name: Coming from GTA
sections.card: If Grand Theft Auto is your reference point, the adjustment is that this game is slow on purpose. Arthur has weight, horses take time to turn, and picking something up is an animation rather than an instant. Shooting your way through a town works for about ninety seconds, and then the law arrives and stays. Wanted levels do not simply expire either: a witness who sees your face turns into a bounty you pay off at a post office. Cover your face for anything illegal, ride rather than sprint, and treat camp as somewhere you go back to rather than a menu.

sections.name: Emotions
sections.card: Moodlets add up into one emotion, and the emotion changes what your Sim can do and how fast they learn. Focused speeds up logic and programming, Inspired speeds up creative skills, Confident unlocks bolder social options. Decorated rooms, showers, tea and thinking at a chess board are the reliable ways to choose the mood you want before starting work.

sections.name: Sad moodlets
sections.card: Sad usually comes from a moodlet with a timer — a death, a rejection, an uncomfortable house — and it overrides better moods until it expires. Check the moodlet list to see which one and how long. A shower, a good meal, comfortable furniture and time with a friend clear the ordinary causes; the grief ones simply have to run out.

sections.name: Raising a skill quickly
sections.card: Three things stack: the matching emotion, a good object to practise on, and no interruptions. Set the mood first, use the best version of the object you can afford, and keep needs topped up so the Sim does not wander off mid-session. Children's skills are separate tracks and level faster.

sections.name: Promotions
sections.card: A promotion wants four things at once: the listed skill levels, the daily task done, good work performance, and a decent mood on the way out the door. The career panel lists exactly which skills and how high. Sending a Sim to work in the right emotion is usually the missing piece.

sections.name: Making money
sections.card: Painting and writing are the classic self-employed earners because they only need one skill and one object, and both scale hard with level. Gardening is slower to start and larger later. Selling collectibles funds the very early game, and a cheap starter lot leaves more for the object that earns.

sections.name: Fires
sections.card: There are no firefighters to call in The Sims 4. Keep a fire extinguisher and a smoke alarm in the kitchen, and when something catches, direct a Sim to extinguish it rather than waiting — panicking Sims will not act on their own. Sims can die in a fire, so getting everyone out of the room is the safer first move.

sections.name: moveobjects
sections.card: Open the cheat console with Ctrl+Shift+C, enter testingcheats true, then bb.moveobjects on. Objects will then place anywhere, ignoring the grid and each other, and Alt while dragging frees the rotation. Things placed this way can end up unusable by Sims, so it is a decorating tool first.

sections.name: Kaos mode and Revolution mode
sections.card: Two different games. Kaos is score attack against a clock in one zone at a time: you extend the time by hitting the objectives that pop up mid-riot rather than by surviving. Revolution is the story — a chain of missions per zone with objectives handed out by the resistance, and it is where characters and zones unlock.

sections.name: Fighting the Corporation
sections.card: Corporation troops shoot from range and arrive in groups, so open ground kills you. Fight along the shopfronts and stalls where you can break line of sight, pick up whatever weapon the last one dropped, and use thrown objects and the crowd as cover. Melee is only for one straggler at a time.

sections.name: Unlocking characters
sections.card: Characters come from Revolution progress, not from Kaos scores. Each one plays the same but they are gated behind clearing missions in the zones, so a run through Revolution is what opens up Kaos rather than the other way round.

sections.name: Mining and the run timer
sections.card: Weapons fire themselves; your job is where to stand and what to mine. Mining is not a side activity — it is where the resources for upgrades come from, so a run spent only kiting is a run that ends underpowered. Each stage runs to a timer and then a descent, with the difficulty stepping up each time.

sections.name: Classes
sections.card: Each dwarf class comes with its own weapon pool and its own movement kit, and that combination decides how you play far more than any single upgrade. Try one class over several runs rather than switching each time: the upgrades that matter are the ones that stack with what the class already does.

sections.name: Upgrades and overclocks
sections.card: Levelling offers a choice of upgrades, and taking a little of everything is the common way to lose. Pick one weapon to carry the run and feed it, then spend the rest on survivability. Overclocks change what a weapon is for rather than making it bigger, so read what one removes as well as what it adds.

sections.name: Exploder
sections.card:
Summary: Large orange glyphids that walk into you and detonate in a wide blast.
Weak points: Fragile, and the blasts chain, so one popped early clears the group behind it.
Tips: Weapons fire themselves, so it dies where you stand - keep distance and the blast lands in the swarm instead.

sections.name: Praetorian
sections.card:
Summary: A large melee glyphid with far more health than anything else in the wave.
Weak points: Slow enough to kite indefinitely while the rest of the swarm is cleared.
Tips: It digs through terrain to reach you, so rock is not a wall - pick the exit lane before it arrives.

sections.name: Acid Spitter
sections.card:
Summary: Ranged glyphids that hold a medium distance, fire purple acid and back away instead of closing in.
Weak points: Fragile, and they retreat rather than fight, so walking at them is what kills them.
Tips: Orbiting a swarm drags you through their fire - turn into the spitters and clear the line.

sections.name: Mactera
sections.card:
Summary: Flying enemies that cross walls, vines and voids as if the terrain were not there.
Weak points: The common ones drift rather than hunt and can be walked around; the elites chase you.
Tips: Mining a pocket does nothing against them, so no dug corridor is safe while Mactera are up.

sections.name: Dreadnought Twins
sections.card:
Summary: Two smaller Dreadnoughts at once - the Lacerator chases and leaps, the Arbalest hangs back firing fireball spreads.
Weak points: Neither is as tough as a full Dreadnought on its own.
Phases: Let their health bars drift apart and both turn immune while they heal the gap closed.
Tips: Split fire evenly rather than burning one down, and the healing never starts.

sections.name: Red Sugar
sections.card:
Summary: The glowing red crystals in the cave walls, mined for an instant heal.
Uses: The only healing during a stage, apart from the gold heal at the shop between stages.
Tips: It cannot be banked, so leave a node standing near where you fight and come back once a wave has hurt you.

sections.name: Nitra
sections.card:
Summary: The resource that pays for weapons rather than for your dwarf.
Uses: Buys weapon upgrade cards at the between-stage shop and rerolls the artifact choice from the Supply Pod.
Tips: No nitra means an underleveled weapon however much gold you mined, so keep mining it for whichever weapon carries the run.

sections.name: Gold
sections.card:
Summary: The general currency, mined from the walls and dropped by lootbugs.
Uses: Buys player stat upgrades between stages, rerolls shop stock and level-up cards, and pays for a fifty percent heal.
Tips: There is no shop after the final stage, so gold still in hand by then only buys rerolls.

sections.name: Dark Link
sections.card:
Summary: Your own shadow, fought in the flooded illusion room partway through the Water Temple.
Weak points: He mirrors and blocks sword attacks but has no answer to the Megaton Hammer or Din's Fire.
Tips: Hammer him as he perches on your held-out blade - trading ordinary swings is what drags the fight out.

sections.name: Phantom Ganon
sections.card:
Summary: The Forest Temple boss, who rides out of the wall paintings before taking to the air.
Weak points: An arrow drops the rider, and his energy ball comes back at him off a plain sword slash.
Phases: Only one of the two riders is real, so watch the paintings rather than the room.
Tips: Keep the rally going until the ball lands, then slash him while he is grounded.

sections.name: Morpha
sections.card:
Summary: The Water Temple boss, an amoeba whose red nucleus swims the flooded room and lashes at you with water tentacles.
Weak points: The nucleus is the only part that can be hurt, and the hookshot drags it onto the floor.
Tips: Pull it in, slash it while it is beached, and fight from a corner so the tentacles come from one side.

sections.name: ReDead and Gibdo
sections.card:
Summary: Corpses whose scream freezes you in place before they grab on and drain hearts, the bandaged Gibdos hitting hardest.
Weak points: The Sun's Song stops any of them where they stand, leaving free hits or a clear walk past.
Tips: Play it as one turns toward you, not after the scream lands, and mash buttons to shake off a grab.

sections.name: Wallmaster
sections.card:
Summary: The giant hand that drops from the ceiling and carries you back to the dungeon entrance.
Weak points: Slow and fragile once landed, so it only threatens you while you are standing still.
Tips: Watch for the shadow spreading on the floor around you, step out of it, then kill it before it climbs back up.

sections.name: Bottles
sections.card:
Summary: Four bottles exist, and what you keep in them matters more than most items.
Uses: A caught fairy revives you the moment you die, Blue Fire from the Ice Cavern melts red ice, and bugs dig up the soil patches hiding Gold Skulltulas.
Tips: Never enter a dungeon with all four empty, since a fairy is the cheapest extra life in the game.

sections.name: Iron Boots
sections.card:
Summary: The boots from the Ice Cavern that sink you to the bottom of any water and hold you against wind.
Uses: Needed to reach and move around the Water Temple, and to push through the gusts in the Shadow Temple.
Tips: The Zora Tunic is what lets you breathe down there, and on N64 the boots are swapped from the equipment menu every time.

sections.name: Hookshot and Longshot
sections.card:
Summary: The Forest Temple gives the Hookshot and the Water Temple upgrades it to the Longshot, which reaches twice as far.
Uses: Pulls you to wood, ladders and marked targets, and drags distant chests, items and Skulltula tokens to you.
Tips: When a ledge looks impossible, look for wood or a target rather than a jump.

sections.name: Late-round rocket enemies
sections.card:
Summary: Late in a round, enemies start showing up with rocket launchers. They are the most dangerous thing on screen and the usual reason a strong run ends.
Tips: Treat one as the priority target the moment it appears, ahead of whatever crowd you are already fighting.

sections.name: Grenade launcher
sections.card:
Summary: The most forgiving of the heavy weapons to actually use on a controller.
Uses: A good default when you want damage without fighting the aiming.
Tips: How easy a weapon is to handle on a pad matters more here than its raw damage.

sections.name: Rocket launcher
sections.card:
Summary: High damage, and the easiest weapon in the game to hurt yourself with.
Uses: Best used at range, into a crowd you are not standing in.
Tips: Fired at close quarters it will take your own health down. Misusing it costs more than the extra damage wins.

sections.name: Flamethrower
sections.card:
Summary: A close-range crowd weapon.
Uses: The suggested approach is to move through a swarm rather than fire into it from outside - circling inside the crowd while it burns.
Tips: Treat this as a tactic to try rather than a settled one. It is an untested lead, not a verified rule.

sections.name: Causing chaos
sections.card:
Summary: Kaos mode scores you on chaos, and new players almost always cause too little of it.
Tips: The most common mistake in the first ten minutes is playing carefully. Damage, crowds and destruction are the point, not something that happens on the way to an objective.

sections.name: Round time and the +15s pickups
sections.card:
Summary: A round runs on a timer, and pickups scattered around the level add +15 seconds each.
Tips: Knowing when to break off and go for time, instead of staying in a fight, is the other thing new players get wrong. A round you extend is worth more than a crowd you finish.

sections.name: Starting out in Black Mesa
sections.card: Black Mesa is Half-Life rebuilt from the ground up on the Source engine, with new art, sound and voice work but the original's chapters, weapons and enemies kept on purpose rather than added to. The one exception is Xen: those chapters are mostly new work and far longer than the 1998 originals, so budget more time for the alien world than veterans remember. Expect the same shape of game throughout: no cutscenes, scripted scenes you walk through, a crowbar for crates and vents, and fights that go better from a doorway than from the middle of a room. There are 25 achievements, Workshop support and a separate deathmatch mode; the campaign itself is single-player only.

sections.name: Tentacles
sections.card: Three blade-headed stalks in the missile silo in Blast Pit, and nothing you carry can kill them: shooting a stalk only drives it into its pit for a moment, and one strike kills you outright. They are blind and hunt by sound and vibration, gently tapping the floor and then hammering wherever they heard you, so crouch-walk past them and never run in the open. A grenade lobbed to the far side of the silo pulls all three heads to the noise while you cross. The chapter's real job is elsewhere: restore power, oxygen and fuel to the rocket motor and fire it, which burns the whole cluster out and opens the tunnels beyond.

sections.name: Gonarch
sections.card: The giant four-legged headcrab mother in the caverns of Xen. Its shell shrugs off almost everything; the pale egg sac swinging under its body is the only part that takes damage, so any shot not at the sac is wasted. At range it lobs white acid mortars from its back, up close its front legs slash for huge damage, and whenever it sees you it births baby headcrabs in pairs, up to twenty alive at once: weak and fast, there to distract you from the sac. It walks the webbing over the pits that you and its children fall straight through, so watch your footing more than its feet. When it dies the sac bursts and releases one last brood, so back away before the pop.

sections.name: Nihilanth
sections.card: The floating giant at the very end. Its head stays shut while the orange energy spheres orbiting it hold a charge, and it refills them from the crystals around the chamber, so the fight is the crystals first: break every one, then wait for the head to open like a flower and shoot the sphere inside, which is the only weak spot. Meanwhile it fires streams of purple bolts, calls in Vortigaunts and Alien Controllers, and throws big green orbs that teleport you into side arenas full of aliens; those orbs can be shot down before they reach you. Keep moving between crystals rather than standing to trade shots.

sections.name: Gargantua
sections.card: Six metres of blue armour with one glowing eye, immune to ordinary bullets and a little faster than you on foot. It cooks anything close with the flame jets in its hands, and its stomp sends a red shockwave along the floor that hits hard but travels slowly, so step sideways rather than backing up. You are not meant to shoot it down; each meeting has a tool nearby. The first one dies to the track power you restore in Sector E, the one in the motorpool dies to the airstrikes you call from the Marines' tactical map, and the one on Xen can be waited out from a crevice once it starts patrolling. If you must fight one, only explosives and energy weapons hurt it: rockets, satchel charges, the Gluon Gun.

sections.name: HECU Marines
sections.card: The soldiers sent in to clean the facility out, including anyone who saw what happened. They fight in squads and keep in touch by radio, throw grenades to flush you out of cover, and some act as medics or engineers for the rest. Where they have dug in they add laser tripmines, sentry guns and manned emplacements, and outdoors they have air support. They carry submachine guns with grenade launchers, shotguns, light machine guns and sniper rifles, so the corridor habits that beat aliens get you killed here: break line of sight, fight one doorway at a time, and check any room they held for red tripmine beams before you walk in.

sections.name: Houndeye
sections.card: Three-legged with one big compound eye, and always in a pack of up to four. Alone one is timid; together they charge a sonic shockwave that hurts you and smashes crates and glass, and the damage rises with the size of the pack. Kill the leader and the rest lose the ability to charge the wave and fall back to a weak bark, so pick out the one the others follow. A resting pack dozes and wakes to noise, which is your chance to line up the first shot. Bullsquids leave them alone, so a room with both is not a three-way fight.

sections.name: Tau Cannon
sections.card: The gauss gun: a particle beam that draws straight from the suit's uranium reserve, shared with the Gluon Gun, so it never reloads. Tap-fire sends fast yellow beams that chew through unarmoured targets; hold the alternate fire to charge a white-hot shot that punches through several enemies or a wall and explodes on the far side, which turns cover into a trap for whoever is behind it. Beams also bounce off walls at shallow angles. Fire the charged shot straight down and the recoil throws you upward, the gauss jump, which reaches ledges nothing else does.

sections.name: Gluon Gun
sections.card: The last weapon in the game, handed over in the Lambda Core test chamber by the scientist who built it and cannot bring himself to use it. It pours out a continuous spiral of energy that destroys most things in seconds, with splash at the point of contact, stays accurate at long range, and goes straight through bulletproof armour, which makes it the one gun that genuinely hurts a Gargantua. It shares the uranium reserve with the Tau Cannon and drinks it fast, so it is not a room-clearing tool; save it for whatever nothing else is denting. It does not work underwater.

sections.name: Hivehand
sections.card: The living alien rifle the Alien Grunts carry, though you cannot take one from a body: one lies past the tripmine room in Surface Tension and another in the Lambda supply depot before the main portal, in case you missed the first. It grows its own ammo, eight hornets loaded at a time and replaced within seconds, and the primary-fire hornets home in on living targets around corners and chase whatever runs. That makes it the free answer to headcrabs, barnacles and Alien Controllers without spending real ammunition. Alternate fire dumps all eight fast and straight, good for barrels and point-blank damage. Hornets ignore anything inorganic and bounce off looking for something alive.

sections.name: Long Jump Module
sections.card: Handed to you at the end of Lambda Core for the world beyond, and the only way across Xen's floating islands, where the gravity is weak and a missed gap drops you into the void. Crouch and then jump in quick succession and the suit launches you a long way forward; the training course taught it, but Xen is where it counts. Take a couple of practice jumps on solid ground before the first real gap so the timing is in your thumbs, not your head.

sections.name: Starting out in Hollow Knight
sections.card: A side-scrolling metroidvania: a huge connected kingdom under the town of Dirtmouth that opens piece by piece as you find abilities. There is no map of an area until you find Cornifer, the humming cartographer, and buy his copy, and it only fills in as you rest at benches once you own a quill from his wife in Dirtmouth. Benches are everything: they save, restore your masks, and are the only place charms can be swapped. Your nail is short, so learn early to bounce off enemies and spikes with a downward slash. Hitting enemies fills the soul meter; hold Focus to spend it healing one mask at a time, or tap it for spells. Dying is not the end: your Shade waits where you fell, holding your Geo.

sections.name: Dying, your Shade and lost Geo
sections.card: When your shell breaks you respawn at the last bench, all your Geo stays behind in a Shade at or just before the room you died in, and your soul meter is cracked to two thirds until you deal with it. Walk back and an off-key music-box tune tells you it is near; it floats at you, swings a nail and casts whichever spells you have learned, and it dies after a handful of hits, returning the Geo and mending the meter. Die again before reaching it and a new Shade replaces the old one, Geo and all, so a big purse is a reason to go back first. If the Shade sits somewhere brutal, Confessor Jiji behind the locked door on the east side of Dirtmouth will summon it to her room for a Rancid Egg.

sections.name: Charms and notches
sections.card: Charms are the build system: each takes a set number of notches, you start with three notches and can find eight more, and you can only swap charms while sitting on a bench. Forty-five exist, though five are upgrades that replace another. Spend early Geo on Salubra's first notch in the Crossroads once you hold five charms. If a charm needs more notches than you have left you can force it in and go overcharmed: every hit you take then does double damage, fine for platforming and a bad idea in a boss room. Early keepers: Soul Catcher from the Ancestral Mound for more healing fuel per hit, and Quick Focus from Salubra, which makes healing a third faster and turns many boss fights.

sections.name: Nail upgrades and Pale Ore
sections.card: The Nailsmith in the City of Tears reforges the nail four times, from 5 damage up to 21: the first upgrade costs Geo alone, the next three need one, two and three Pale Ore on top, six Ore in all, scattered across the kingdom behind bosses, grubs and hidden rooms. The Mantis Lords are a good deadline for the first upgrade. The nail also carries you: a downward slash on enemies, spikes and the purple mushrooms of the Fungal Wastes bounces you upward, which is both a combat rhythm and the way into places you are not supposed to reach yet. Mark of Pride from the Mantis Village adds a quarter to its reach.

sections.name: Soul, Focus and spells
sections.card: Every nail hit on an enemy adds soul to the round meter on the left, up to ninety-nine. Hold Focus to turn thirty-three soul into one mask of health; it takes over a second, you stand still for it, and a hit cancels it, so heal during a boss's long, far-away attacks and not on hope. Tap the cast button instead and the same soul fuels spells: Vengeful Spirit from the Ancestral Mound fires forward and early on hits three times as hard as your nail, Desolate Dive from the Soul Sanctum slams down, breaks fragile floors and makes you briefly untouchable, and Howling Wraiths blasts upward and around you. Hot springs refill soul fast and slowly top up masks; a bench refills the soul totems you can hit for a free meter.

sections.name: Movement abilities and where they are
sections.card: Hallownest opens in the order you find its abilities, and knowing that order saves hours of poking at walls. The Mothwing Cloak, a short dash with a brief cooldown, is Hornet's prize in Greenpath. The Mantis Claw, wall-cling and wall-jump, waits in the Mantis Village below the Fungal Wastes. The Crystal Heart, a charged horizontal flight from the ground or a wall, is in the mines of Crystal Peak. The Monarch Wings, a double jump, lie at the bottom of the Ancient Basin. Isma's Tear lets you swim in acid and opens the Waterways and several shortcuts; the Shade Cloak from the Abyss upgrades the dash to pass through enemies, their attacks and the black Shade Gates. If a gap looks impossible, it usually is until one of these.

sections.name: False Knight
sections.card: The armoured maggot in the Forgotten Crossroads, and the first real fight. He leaps, charges, and slams a mace that sends a shockwave along the whole floor; jump the wave rather than backing off. Hitting the armour earns no soul, so save what you have for healing: the only time you gain soul or do real damage is when the armour empties and he topples, exposing the maggot's head. Pile hits on the head, then back off, because he wakes into a rage that rains barrels; those barrels can be knocked back into him for ten damage each and can even stagger him. After the third exposure he breaks the floor and falls below; drop after him and finish the maggot. If it goes badly, a wall above the left gate becomes breakable after his first rage, and the Vengeful Spirit spell is in the very next room, which makes the rematch far easier.

sections.name: Hornet in Greenpath
sections.card: The fight for the dash, at the Lake of Unn end of Greenpath. She lunges along the ground, dives from the air, throws her needle across most of the arena and pulls it back (it cuts on the return too), and spins a thread storm around herself. She stands still for about a second while she takes her stance, so open with upward slashes. Trade a few nail hits when she lunges in, then hit her with Vengeful Spirit when she backs off; at this point the spell does three times your nail's damage. After roughly a fifth of her health she kneels to recover: heal then, or spend a spell on her, because the next hit wakes her, and she always leaps after a stagger, which is a free window. Heal during the needle throw or the thread storm, both short-ranged and slow. Mistime a jump over the needle and a downward slash bounces you off it safely.

sections.name: Mantis Lords
sections.card: The three sisters on the thrones in the Mantis Village do not attack until you challenge them, and then a cage closes with spike pits either side. One fights first: a lance dash along the whole floor, a drop from directly above you, and a spinning boomerang blade thrown from the wall in a rising or falling arc. Each attack ends with her vanishing, so the rhythm is dodge, one or two hits, reset; the attacks quicken as she weakens. Heal during the boomerang, the slowest attack. When she yields the other two fight together, sometimes dashing from both ends at once; stand near the centre when they throw the short-arc boomerangs and the blades pass over you, long enough to heal two masks. Go in with at least one nail upgrade and Quick Focus if you have it. Win and the whole village stands down, a bench opens, and Mark of Pride waits in a chest to the northeast.

sections.name: Soul Master
sections.card: Top of the Soul Sanctum in the City of Tears. He teleports between every attack: a dash across the arena, a homing soul orb that will not hit you if you stand right beside him, a ring of four orbs he glides across with (and which boomerang back after he vanishes), and a dive slam that sends shockwaves both ways, sometimes faked once before landing above your new spot. Hit him from below while he is conjuring orbs; that is the open window. When he deflates and gasps he is staggered, and there is a moment to hit him without ending the stagger. He plays dead once, leaves the Desolate Dive spell as bait, and comes back through the roof for a faster second round with far less time to heal, so learn the dodges in round one.

sections.name: Watcher Knights
sections.card: Six armoured husks at the top of the Watcher's Spire, fought at most two at a time; a new one wakes twenty seconds after the last, or two together if you kill fast. Each does a double slash, rolls as a ball along the floor and bounces after you, and is immune to the nail while rolling (spells still land). Their only answer to attacks from above is that bouncing roll, so fight from the air and never let them corner you. Before the fight, break the hidden wall on the approach and cut the chandelier's support: it drops on the second husk from the left and you fight five instead of six. Quick Focus matters here; Desolate Dive with Shaman Stone kills one in three casts while keeping you untouchable.

sections.name: Broken Vessel
sections.card: The infected husk shaped like you, far west in the Ancient Basin past a gap that needs the Crystal Heart. It dashes with slashes that cover most of the arena, flails its nail overhead, leaps to slam down and throw four arcs of infection, shakes out a cascade of blobs that covers nearly everything when its health gets low, and spawns weak balloons that drift at you. It is one of the few bosses that gets knocked back, so Vengeful Spirit can hit it twice; Desolate Dive during the cascade both damages it and keeps you safe. A longer nail (Mark of Pride or Longnail) matches its reach, and Defender's Crest quietly clears the balloons. Heal when it staggers, head weighed down and shaking.

sections.name: Primal Aspid
sections.card: The flying spitter of Kingdom's Edge and the Colosseum, and by common agreement the nastiest ordinary enemy in the game. It hovers just out of nail reach and spits three blobs in a spread with the middle one aimed at you, so close range is worse, not better. Listen for the whistle of its wings and deal with it before anything else in the room; nail arts, especially Great Slash or Dash Slash, reach it when normal swings will not, and a spell does the job from range. In the Colosseum they are the first thing to kill in any wave.

genre_patterns.card: Soulslike basics: learn dodge timing, stamina management, and safe heal windows. Summon allies when available; upgrade vigor before glass-cannon damage.
